summary: This standards-track document defines a standard algorithm to temporarily postpone, or back off, SPF computations in link-state IGPs. It reduces load and churn on nodes when several close-together events would otherwise cause many calculations. A single standard algorithm helps networks behave predictably.

plainLanguage.summary: If many small changes happen fast, redo the map once instead of each time. This tells routers to wait a bit.

questions: how to delay spf calculations in ospf and is-is
what are the default spf delay values
what is a micro-loop in igp convergence
subtitle: A standard wait-and-see timer scheme for when link-state routers recompute routes after network changes.

tldr.problem: Link-state routers recompute routes after each change. Fast reaction is good for one failure, but many close-together events cause heavy computation, and different vendors' back-off algorithms leave routers out of step.
tldr.mechanism: A three-state machine (QUIET, SHORT_WAIT, LONG_WAIT) with three timers picks the delay before each SPF computation: short for the first event, a bit longer for related events, long when the network is unstable.
tldr.outcome: All routers using the same algorithm and values delay the same amount, which reduces the probability and duration of transient micro-loops. It does not prevent all of them.

today: RFC 8405 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Routers Need to Back Off
sections.content:
Link-state IGPs such as IS-IS, OSPF and OSPFv3 compute routes in a distributed way. For consistent routing tables, all routers need the same version of the link-state database and need to compute at about the same time.

When the network is stable, a router should start a new Shortest Path First (SPF) computation as soon as it detects a failure. During repeated failures, though, limiting the frequency saves control plane resources and reduces churn in LDP, RSVP-TE, BGP, fast reroute computations and FIB updates.

IGPs usually implement an SPF back-off algorithm, but different implementations chose different ones. In a multi-vendor network, routers then delay by different amounts, which raises the chance that they compute from different database versions and so raises the probability and duration of micro-loops. This document specifies one standard algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine everyone in a class redrawing the same map. If they all wait the same time before redrawing, they stay in sync. This RFC picks the waiting rules.

sections.title: Goals of the Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm has four high-level goals:

  • very fast convergence for a single event such as a link failure;
  • paced fast convergence for several close events while the IGP is considered stable enough;
  • delayed convergence when the IGP is unstable, so resources are conserved;
  • avoiding different SPF_DELAY values across routers in the same area or level, even though routers may hear about events at different times or in different orders.
sections.plainLanguage: React instantly to one small problem, calmly to a few, and slowly when everything is going wrong. And make sure everybody does it the same way.

sections.title: Delays and Intervals
sections.content:
An IGP event is the reception or origination of a link-state database change that requires a new routing table computation, such as a topology, prefix or metric change. Locally triggering a computation is not an IGP event. The type of computation (full SPF, incremental SPF or Partial Route Computation) is a local matter.

SPF_DELAY is the time from the first triggering event to the start of the computation. It takes one of three values:

  • INITIAL_SPF_DELAY: very small, to handle an isolated link failure quickly (example: 0 milliseconds).
  • SHORT_SPF_DELAY: small, for a single component failure that causes several events, such as a node or SRLG failure (example: 50-100 milliseconds).
  • LONG_SPF_DELAY: long, used when the IGP is unstable (example: 2 seconds).

Two intervals complete the picture. TIME_TO_LEARN_INTERVAL is the maximum time typically needed to learn all events from one component failure (example: 1 second). HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL is how long with no events before the IGP counts as stable and the delay returns to INITIAL_SPF_DELAY (example: 3 seconds). It MUST be longer than TIME_TO_LEARN_INTERVAL.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three waiting times: a tiny wait, a short wait and a long wait. Two stopwatches decide when to switch between them.

sections.title: Principles Behind the Delays
sections.content:
The first event is assumed to be a single simple change, so the router delays only by INITIAL_SPF_DELAY. That is the most common case in a typical network.

If more events arrive within TIME_TO_LEARN_INTERVAL, the assumption is that one component failed but needs several events to be fully known. Waiting for all of them lets the IGP compute the post-failure table in a single further computation, so SHORT_SPF_DELAY is used.

If events keep arriving after TIME_TO_LEARN_INTERVAL from the first event received in the QUIET state, the network probably has multiple independent failures. LONG_SPF_DELAY is then used until no events have arrived for HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL.

The algorithm is driven by elapsed time from the initial event, not by the number of computations performed. Different routers may receive events at different times, so they cannot be assumed to perform the same number of computations.
sections.plainLanguage: One bump: fix it right away. A few bumps close together: wait a moment to see them all. Bumps keep coming: wait a long while until things calm down.

sections.title: The SPF Delay State Machine
sections.content:
The finite state machine starts in QUIET with all three timers (SPF_TIMER, HOLDDOWN_TIMER, LEARN_TIMER) off. SHORT_WAIT is entered when an event arrives in QUIET. LONG_WAIT is entered when LEARN_TIMER expires in SHORT_WAIT.

The transitions are:

  • 1: event in QUIET starts SPF_TIMER with INITIAL_SPF_DELAY (if not running), starts LEARN_TIMER and HOLDDOWN_TIMER, and moves to SHORT_WAIT.
  • 2: event in SHORT_WAIT resets HOLDDOWN_TIMER and starts SPF_TIMER with SHORT_SPF_DELAY if not running.
  • 3: LEARN_TIMER expiry moves to LONG_WAIT.
  • 4: event in LONG_WAIT resets HOLDDOWN_TIMER and starts SPF_TIMER with LONG_SPF_DELAY if not running.
  • 5: HOLDDOWN_TIMER expiry in LONG_WAIT moves to QUIET.
  • 6: HOLDDOWN_TIMER expiry in SHORT_WAIT deactivates LEARN_TIMER and moves to QUIET.
  • 7, 8, 9: SPF_TIMER expiry in QUIET, SHORT_WAIT or LONG_WAIT computes SPF and stays in the same state.
sections.plainLanguage: The router is like a person who is calm, then alert, then in a long wait-it-out mode. Quiet time brings it back to calm.

sections.title: Configuration and Default Values
sections.content:
All parameters MUST be configurable per protocol instance and MAY be configurable per LSDB (an IS-IS level or OSPF area). The delays SHOULD be configurable with millisecond granularity and MUST be configurable with at least a tenth of a second. The range SHOULD run from 0 milliseconds to at least 6000 milliseconds.

If the algorithm is enabled by default, these defaults SHOULD be used: INITIAL_SPF_DELAY 50 ms, SHORT_SPF_DELAY 200 ms, LONG_SPF_DELAY 5000 ms, TIME_TO_LEARN_INTERVAL 500 ms and HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL 10000 ms.

Operators are RECOMMENDED to keep INITIAL_SPF_DELAY <= SHORT_SPF_DELAY <= LONG_SPF_DELAY. In case of doubt, choose conservatively (longer values). To mitigate micro-loops, all routers in the domain, or at least in the same area or level, are RECOMMENDED to use exactly the same values.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of suggested waiting times so that routers from different makers wait the same amount by default.

sections.title: Partial Deployment and Micro-loops
sections.content:
The algorithm helps against micro-loops only if deployed with the same parameters on all routers in the domain or at least the area or level. Where a previous algorithm was used uniformly, partial deployment will increase the frequency and duration of micro-loops. Migrating all routers at roughly the same time is therefore RECOMMENDED.

Micro-loops come from unsynchronized or unordered FIB updates, which involve flooding, SPF wait time, computation, FIB distribution and FIB update. This document addresses only the SPF wait time. It does not prevent all micro-loops, but it is less complex and costly than full solutions such as distributed tunnels, synchronized FIB update or the ordered FIB approach.
sections.plainLanguage: If only some routers follow the new waiting rule, they get out of step. So everyone should switch about the same time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The algorithm does not compromise IGP security. An attacker able to generate IGP events could delay IGP convergence, but the LONG_SPF_DELAY state may help mitigate the effects of Denial-of-Service attacks that generate many events. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone keeps poking the router, it learns to wait longer instead of working itself to exhaustion.
